The Australian anchovy (Engraulis australis) is a small pelagic clupeiform fish widely distributed across temperate coastal waters of southern Australia. Adult individuals of this species attain a maximum recorded standard length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a modest size relative to many other engraulids. At a stable water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation to the moment of chorion rupture is remarkably brief, with hatching occurring just 5 days [ab = 5 days] after spawning. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, is extremely small; based on morphometric relationships derived from the egg dimensions of related species, the estimated dry weight at birth is approximately 0.0003 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0003 grams]. This lecithotrophic stage persists only briefly as the larva rapidly depletes its yolk supply and commences the critical transition to exogenous feeding, a period of high mortality in the wild.

Sexual maturation in Engraulis australis is attained at a comparatively small body size. Field surveys and histological analyses of gonadal tissue indicate that the standard length at puberty is reached at approximately 6.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6.5 centimeters], a threshold that is commonly achieved within the first year of life for fast-growing cohorts. At the same experimental temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the maximum lifespan of this species has been estimated at roughly 6 years [am = roughly 6 years], although field records of otolith-based ages suggest that few individuals in natural populations live beyond three to four years due to predation pressure. The modest ultimate body size of this species is further reflected in its maximum adult wet weight, calculated from length-weight regressions to be 21.3 grams [Wwi = 21.3 grams]. Females in spawning condition typically exhibit a robust, gravid body form.

Reproductive output in the Australian anchovy is substantial for a fish of its size. Maximum documented fecundity was derived from studies on the congener Engraulis mordax and applied to this species, revealing that at the species' preferred thermal regime of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], individual females produce approximately 301 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 301 eggs per day] when translating the annualised reproductive rate across the spawning season. This high daily fecundity is sustained by a protracted spawning period in which adults can release eggs over many months. Spawning events are frequent, with females capable of releasing multiple batches of pelagic, transparent, yolk-laden ova in rapid succession. The combination of a high egg production rate and a long breeding season allows large numbers of offspring to be generated annually, supporting the species' role as a critical forage fish in coastal pelagic food webs.

The early life-history traits of Engraulis australis reflect a strategy of rapid development and high fecundity typical of small, short-lived pelagic teleosts. At a temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the age at birth is just 5 days [ab = 5 days], a value consistent with observations in the European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus under similar thermal conditions. Hatchlings are tiny, with a dry weight at birth of approximately 0.0003 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0003 grams], a mass that constrains their initial nutritional reserves. The yolk-sac larva, or alevin phase, is thus exceedingly brief, lasting only a few days before the mouth opens and the larva commences first exogenous feeding on small planktonic prey. This rapid transition is critical for survival, as the point of no return is quickly reached if prey is unavailable. Larval growth during the subsequent pelagic phase is strongly temperature-dependent.

From an ecological perspective, the life history of Engraulis australis is tightly coupled to its thermal environment. At the characteristic temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], individuals are predicted to have a maximum longevity of 6 years [am = 6 years], a duration that appears brief compared to many demersal fishes but is typical of small, plankton-feeding forage species. The ultimate standard length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] and the standard length at puberty of 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters] together describe a life cycle in which somatic growth is rapid early in life, allowing the onset of reproductive activity at less than half the maximum size. The maximum adult wet weight of 21.3 grams [Wwi = 21.3 grams] and the correspondingly small dry weight at birth of approximately 0.0003 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0003 grams] represent a substantial nine-orders-of-magnitude increase in mass from egg to adult, underscoring the high growth rates and elevated metabolic demands that characterise this species' energetic budget.
